notes.meaning: After three days of prayer and fasting, Esther dressed in her finest royal robes and entered the courtyard outside the king's hall. She could be put to death for coming without an invite, but she bravely stepped out in faith. Her choice of royal clothing showed proper respect for the king while seeking his attention. When we face big challenges, seeking God first gives us quiet courage.

As soon as the king saw Esther, God gave her favor in the king's eyes. He held out his golden royal rod, called a scepter, to show she was forgiven and welcome. Esther walked forward and touched the tip of it in humble respect and gratitude.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: In the ancient Greek additions found in Catholic Bibles, Esther was so terrified by the king's fierce look that she fainted, prompting God to soften the king's heart so he rushed from his throne to comfort her.

notes.meaning: The king knew Esther had risked her life to see him, so he asked what she needed. He offered to grant her wish even up to half of his kingdom. This was an ancient royal saying that simply meant he was ready to be very generous.

Instead of blurting out her difficult problem right away, Esther politely invited the king and Haman to a private dinner that day. Inviting Haman kept him from suspecting anything while giving her a private setting to plead her case. She used wisdom and patience to prepare the king's heart.

The king ordered his servants to fetch Haman quickly so they could grant Esther's wish. Both the king and Haman then came to the feast Esther had prepared. Everything was moving forward smoothly under God's quiet guidance.

While they were relaxing and drinking wine at the end of the meal, the king repeated his big promise. He urged Esther to tell him her real wish, promising again that she could have whatever she asked. He knew the meal was only the doorway to her true request.

Esther started to speak but then asked the king and Haman to come to a second banquet the next day. She promised she would finally make her request known at that time. This short delay was guided by God, setting the stage for events that night that would completely turn the tables on Haman.

Haman left the palace feeling proud and on top of the world because of the queen's special invitation. His joy vanished instantly when he saw Mordecai sitting at the palace gate without standing up or trembling before him. Mordecai trusted the Lord and refused to honor an enemy of God's people, which filled Haman with fury.

Even though Haman burned with anger, he controlled his temper for the moment and went home. God's hand kept Haman from harming Mordecai on the spot. Once inside his house, Haman gathered his friends and his wife Zeresh to talk about his feelings.

Haman bragged to his family and friends about his enormous wealth, his many sons, and all his high honors from the king. In ancient Persia, having many sons and great wealth was considered the highest kind of success. Yet Haman used these blessings only to boost his own pride.

Haman boasted that Queen Esther had chosen only him to dine with the king, and that he was invited back again tomorrow. He thought this proved he was completely secure and deeply loved by both rulers. He had no idea that the very dinner he boasted about was being prepared for his downfall.

Haman admitted that none of his riches, honor, or royal favors brought him any real happiness as long as Mordecai sat at the gate refusing to bow. A proud heart can never be satisfied because even the smallest slight ruins all its pleasure. Real peace is found in God, not in human praise.

Zeresh and Haman's friends urged him to build a giant wooden stake seventy-five feet high and ask the king in the morning to have Mordecai executed on it. They told him that once Mordecai was dead, he could enjoy the queen's banquet with a carefree heart. The cruel plan delighted Haman, and he immediately ordered the construction to begin.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars note that the ancient Persian penalty referred to by the Hebrew word for tree or gallows was impalement on a sharpened pole rather than hanging by the neck.
